extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers interested in William S. Burroughs and experimental/avant-garde writing
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and production techniques described on a biographical/wiki page about William S. Burroughs — useful for understanding how to evaluate or emulate his experimental writing (cut-ups, fragmentation, multimedia practice, occult/magical intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew Arnold's criteria for criticism (as endorsed by Burroughs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matthew Arnold set up three criteria for criticism: 1. What is the writer trying to do? 2. How well does he succeed in doing it? 3. Does the work exhibit 'high seriousness' (i.e., does it touch on basic issues of good and evil, life and death and the human condition). Burroughs adds a fourth criterion: 'Write about what you know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burroughs preferred to be evaluated against such objective criteria rather than reviewers' personal prejudices. Use these four points as a framework when judging or reviewing work: identify authorial intent, measure execution, assess seriousness/weight, and check authorial knowledge/authority on subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-up technique as a functional/magical method
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs insisted 'the cut ups are not for artistic purposes' and attributed to them a magical function: they were used for 'political warfare, scientific research, personal therapy, magical divination, and conjuration' with the essential idea that cut-ups 'break down the barriers that surround consciousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or evaluating cut-ups, emphasize intended function (e.g., divination, psychological work, political intervention) over mere novelty. Look for whether cut-ups are deployed to reveal unexpected meaning, to disrupt control systems, or to provoke shifts in perception; avoid treating them as purely decorative or accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-compositional fragmentation (write straight, then chop)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some works (e.g., Cities of the Red Night), Burroughs 'wrote as a straight narrative and then chopped up into a more random pattern, leaving the reader to sort through the characters and events.' This differed from earlier cut-ups that were accidental from the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a technique: compose coherent material first, then fragment/rearrange deliberately to create nonlinearity while retaining some underlying narrative logic. As an evaluative point: assess how successfully the post-hoc chopping balances intelligibility and disorientation; consider whether the rearrangement serves thematic or mythic aims rather than gratuitous obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing as deliberate magical/performative act
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs argued that 'all art is magical in origin' and that writing (through precise and incantatory arrangement of language) is intended 'to produce very definite results' — e.g., invocation, violation of conditioning, or other psychic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or produce prose with attention to its intended effect on readers (ritual, invocation, psychological change). Techniques that read as 'incantatory'—repetitions, precise sonic/lexical arrangements, ritualized structures—should be judged on their ability to produce targeted effects, not merely stylistic flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cut-ups to reveal prescient or meaningful juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs maintained that when you make cut-ups 'you do not get simply random juxtapositions of words, that they do mean something,' and that sometimes these meanings refer to future events or later-recognized connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying or appraising cut-ups, consider claims of emergent meaning: does the rearrangement produce resonant associations, synchronicities, or openings toward new interpretation? Be cautious of overclaiming divination, but note where cut-ups generate unexpectedly coherent thematic or symbolic links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating photography and images as mnemonic/time-image devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs used photography extensively as both a recording medium for planning writings and as a significant element in his artistic practice, photographing and rephotographing images in increasingly complex time-image arrangements and incorporating photographs into cut-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photographs and repeated re-photographing to manipulate memory, temporality, and image-text relations. Evaluate such work by how effectively the visual procedures serve the text's temporal or mnemonic aims and by the integration of images into the cut-up or collage process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with multimedia (sound, film, music, visual art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs branched into multimedia — film, sound recording, spoken-word albums, collaborations with musicians and performers — often as part of an 'experiment and subversion' phase that increased political content and expanded media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess multimedia projects for how well different media modalities extend or transform the literary material (e.g., voice, soundtrack, visual staging) rather than merely accompanying it. As a practice, collaborate across disciplines to amplify experimental aims, political messaging, or ritual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic period: Early work — straightforward linear narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Burroughs's early work (early 1950s: Junkie, Queer, The Yage Letters) are described as relatively straightforward linear narratives concerned with his time in Mexico City and South America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating early-period Burroughs or emulations thereof, expect and assess clarity of narrative, chronological coherence, and intimate subject knowledge; judge success on traditional narrative criteria (plot, character, verisimilitude) rather than experimental fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic period: Cut-up period — fragmentary 'routines' and cut-up/fold-in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mid-1950s to mid-1960s: works (Naked Lunch, The Soft Machine, Nova Express, The Ticket That Exploded) are fragmentary collections of 'routines' and employ cut-up and fold-in techniques, forming the 'Cut-Up Trilogy' and a mythology for the space age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these works on how effectively fragments cohere into mythic or thematic structures, the innovative use of language and montage, and the degree to which fragmentation serves conceptual aims rather than mere shock or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic period: Experiment and subversion — political content and multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Mid-1960s to mid-1970s: continued experimental writing with increased political content and branching into multimedia (film, sound), exemplified by The Third Mind; includes numerous essays, short stories, and collaborative works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works from this period on the interplay between formal experimentation and political intent: does the experimental form clarify or advance political critique? Judge multimedia experiments for coherence between message and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic period: Red Night trilogy — mature mythology and time-travel narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Mid-1970s to mid-1980s: the Red Night trilogy (Cities of the Red Night, The Place of Dead Roads, The Western Lands) creates a complete mythology with time-travel adventures in which narrators rewrite episodes from history to reform mankind; these works were written as straight narratives and then reorganized into non-linear forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the trilogy or similar mythopoeic experiments, focus on the construction and consistency of the invented mythology, the effectiveness of temporal reworkings, and the balance between narrative intelligibility and mythic/ritualistic ambition.
